Docs

Learn to build, one recipe at a time

Friendly, step-by-step lessons for anyone starting out. Each one is a recipe: what you need, the steps in order, and a way to taste-test your result.

New to building things with code? Good. You don’t need any experience, only curiosity. Every lesson is written like a recipe card, so you always know what you’ll make, what you need, and how to check that it worked.

Why adobo?

Adobo is one of the most loved Filipino dishes, and every family makes it a little differently. A simple version needs just ten ingredients: chicken, soy sauce, vinegar, black pepper, sugar, bay leaf, garlic, onion, water and oil. Building a website is the same kind of thing: a few simple ingredients, some heat, and a lot of tasting and adjusting. So each lesson compares the tricky ideas to cooking, and then you make it your own.

The kitchen map

In the kitchenOn the website
The ingredients on the counterHTML: the content and structure of a page
The seasoning: soy sauce, vinegar, garlicCSS or Tailwind: how the page looks
The heat that makes it cookJavaScript or Alpine.js: what makes the page react
Tasting and adjusting as you goTesting and fixing: try it, look, change it
Your recipe notebookGit: saving each version, like “adobo v2, less vinegar”
The kitchen behind the scenesA backend like Laravel: the part visitors never see

Pick a path

Start with the first path if you’re brand new. Inside a path, go in order: each lesson builds on the one before it, and you’ll end up with something real that you made yourself.

Start cooking

Build your first web page, from a blank file to something that reacts.

  1. 1 Your first website Make a real web page from nothing. HTML is where every website starts, like laying out your ingredients before you cook. 15 minutes
  2. 2 Make it taste good Add colour, size and space with Tailwind CSS. Same ingredients, very different dish. 20 minutes
  3. 3 Bring it to life Make your page react to clicks with Alpine.js. This is the heat that makes the pot start to simmer. 20 minutes
  4. 4 Keep your recipe notebook Save every version of your work with Git, and share it on GitHub, like a notebook of recipes you never lose. 25 minutes

The kitchen behind the scenes

Meet Laravel and build a small menu app with pages, a database and forms.

  1. 1 Set up the kitchen Set up Laravel with Herd and serve your first pages. This is the kitchen that cooks each order when it arrives. 25 minutes
  2. 2 Serve a menu Send data to a page and show it with Blade. The kitchen fills in a menu board from a list of dishes. 25 minutes
  3. 3 Hire a waiter Move the cooking out of your routes and into a controller. The route takes the order, and the waiter carries it to the kitchen. 25 minutes
  4. 4 Set the table Give every page the same look with a layout, and reuse small pieces with Blade components. 30 minutes
  5. 5 Stock the pantry Move your dishes out of the code and into a real database, using a migration, a model and a seeder. 35 minutes
  6. 6 Take an order Let a visitor add a dish with a form. Check what they send, show friendly errors, and save it to the database. 35 minutes
  7. 7 Change the menu Finish your menu app. Edit a dish, remove one, and tidy the code so the add and edit forms share the same fields. 40 minutes

Talk to your guests

Build a chatbot in Python, from a simple bot to a real AI one powered by Google’s Gemini.

  1. 1 Your first chatbot Write a small chatbot in Python that answers questions about adobo. No AI needed yet, only rules. 20 minutes
  2. 2 Give it a memory Teach your bot to remember your name, keep its answers in a tidy list, and save the conversation to a file. 25 minutes
  3. 3 Meet Gemini Get a free Gemini API key, keep it safe, and ask Google’s AI your first question from Python. 25 minutes
  4. 4 Give it a personality Use a system instruction to turn Gemini into AdoboBot, with a voice, a style and clear limits. 20 minutes
  5. 5 Chat with Gemini Turn AdoboBot into a real conversation that remembers what you said earlier, and greets each guest by name. 30 minutes
  6. 6 Teach it your recipe Give AdoboBot your own recipe to answer from, and make it handle problems gracefully when the kitchen gets busy. 35 minutes

Cook with electricity

Make lights blink, read buttons and dials, and build your own kitchen timer with an Arduino.

  1. 1 Blink a light Make a light blink with an Arduino. It’s the “hello world” of electronics, and you’ll be surprised how good it feels. 25 minutes
  2. 2 Measure with sound Use an ultrasonic sensor to measure distance. Your Arduino sends out a sound you can’t hear and listens for the echo. 30 minutes
  3. 3 Press a button Add a push button to your circuit, so the Arduino can listen to you as well as talk. Then turn it into a light switch that remembers. 30 minutes
  4. 4 Dim the flame Go beyond on and off. Fade an LED smoothly, using a trick called PWM. 25 minutes
  5. 5 Turn the dial Read a knob with a potentiometer, and use it to control how bright a light is. 30 minutes
  6. 6 Build a kitchen timer Put it all together. Turn a dial to set the minutes, press a button to start, and a light and buzzer tell you when your adobo is ready. 40 minutes

Count the groceries

Use Google Sheets to organise numbers, make charts, look things up and clean up messy data.

  1. 1 Your first spreadsheet Turn a grocery list into a spreadsheet that does the counting for you, using Google Sheets. 20 minutes
  2. 2 Sort, filter and summarise Find answers in a table of sales. Sort it, filter it, and build a summary in a few clicks. 25 minutes
  3. 3 Turn numbers into pictures Make charts in Google Sheets, and learn which kind of chart answers which question. 25 minutes
  4. 4 Let the sheet decide Use IF to make a sheet tell you what to do, and colour the cells that need attention. 30 minutes
  5. 5 Look things up Keep your prices in one place, and let orders find them with XLOOKUP. Change a price once, and everything updates. 30 minutes
  6. 6 Clean up messy data Real data is messy. Fix spaces and capital letters, remove duplicates, and split one column into two. 30 minutes
